title: Inheritance versus composition in JavaScript
hook: Prototype chains make inheritance easy to write and hard to change. Most production JavaScript favors composition — wiring behavior through objects and functions instead of deep class trees.

blocks.text: **Inheritance** (is-a) links types through the prototype chain: `class LtiHandler extends AuthHandler`. **Composition** (has-a) builds objects by combining collaborators: an `AttemptWorker` holds an `attemptStore` and a `clock` rather than extending a `BaseWorker` mega-class. JavaScript supports both; module boundaries and testability usually favor composition.

entries.plainDefinition: Building behavior by combining objects or functions rather than subclassing.
Copying or delegating methods from one object onto another — simulated multiple inheritance.
Forwarding property lookup to another object via [[Prototype]] or explicit forwarding.
Subtype relationship — LtiHandler is an AuthHandler. Use sparingly when behavior truly specializes.

blocks.text: Deep inheritance hierarchies in JavaScript share the same fragility as in C#: base class changes ripple to all descendants, and shared prototype mutation affects every instance. Microservice workers, React hooks, and Node middleware stacks compose small units. **Mixins** and **factory functions** avoid the diamond problem JavaScript never had for classes — but create naming collisions instead.

blocks.title: Prefer composition at application boundaries
blocks.body: Inject stores, clients, and clocks through constructors or parameters. Reserve extends for genuine shared polymorphic behavior with a small, stable surface — not for code reuse alone.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Identify shared behavior
items.body: If two types need the same helper, extract a function or small module — not a BaseService class.

items.title: Wire collaborators in constructor
items.body: `this.store = store` — the instance has-a store. Tests pass mock stores without subclassing.

items.title: Use inheritance only for polymorphic overrides
items.body: When callers hold a base reference and need runtime-specific parse logic, a shallow class hierarchy can fit.

items.title: Avoid prototype mutation in libraries
items.body: Patching `Array.prototype` or shared `.prototype` objects is composition's evil twin — global side effects.

diagram.title: Inheritance versus composition
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  NEED[Need shared behavior] --> Q{True is-a?}
  Q -->|yes small surface| EXT[extends + super\nprototype chain]
  Q -->|no| COMP[composition\ninject deps]
  COMP --> FN[plain functions]
  COMP --> FACT[factory objects]
  EXT --> RISK[fragile base changes]

snippet.explanation: Line 1–5: reusable method bundle. Line 11: mixin copies log onto Service.prototype — shared function, not subclass. Line 14: this refers to instance; constructor.name from class.

blocks.title: When to use which
rows: Factory + object literals / classes with injection
Protected methods on abstract base — one base class limit
Avoid — extension methods on static types

blocks.title: BaseService anti-pattern
blocks.body: A fat `BaseWorker` with database, logging, and HTTP helpers forces every worker into one hierarchy. Extract services and compose them — same advice as C# microservices.

blocks.title: Mixin name collisions
blocks.body: Two mixins defining the same method name — last assign wins silently. TypeScript interfaces do not solve runtime collisions.

blocks.text: JavaScript's single inheritance pushes teams toward **functional composition** (Ramda-style) or **object composition** (React hooks combining state + effects). **Prototype delegation** via `Object.create` implements behavior sharing without classes — used in some DSLs. **Class extends** is still valid for framework integration (Error subclasses, DOM APIs). The interview answer: default to **has-a** for services; use **is-a** when you need shared prototype methods and instanceof checks with a **sealed** small hierarchy. C# adds **interfaces** for multiple contracts; JS has duck typing and optional TypeScript structural checks — no runtime interface.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Many mixins — collision and order bugs

snippet.label: Failure mode — fragile base class constructor
snippet.explanation: Line 3: base calls virtual-like init from constructor. Line 14: derived init runs before derived constructor assigns store — same trap as C# virtual from base ctor.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Always reaching for extends to reuse code — shows OOP habit without JS pragmatism. Patching built-in prototypes as a mixin strategy — breaks libraries. Claiming JS has interface implementation like C# — duck typing only at runtime.

interviewTakeaways: Default to composition (has-a) for services; use inheritance (is-a) for small polymorphic hierarchies.
Mixins copy behavior onto prototypes — watch for method name collisions.
Deep class trees are fragile; factory functions with injected deps test better.

60s: JS single inheritance via prototype chain. Compose dependencies for workers and APIs. extends when callers need polymorphic methods on a shared prototype. Mixins are a compromise. Same BaseService smell as C#.
Follow-up: how would you refactor a three-level class hierarchy into composition?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'Inheritance is the primary reuse mechanism in JS.' Strong: functions and composition are default; extends for true subtype polymorphism.
Calling overridable methods from base constructor — derived state not initialized yet.
Mixin collisions — Object.assign last-wins with no compile-time warning.

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# comparison: Same DI pattern: wire IAttemptStore in constructor rather than inheriting BaseService.
TS interfaces encourage composition at compile time; runtime is still plain object wiring.
